result:
A thousand words is a strange sort of wealth. Enough to be extravagant, not enough to be careless. Roughly the length of a newspaper column, or four pages of a paperback, or the eulogy you'd give if you loved someone but didn't want to keep everyone standing in the cold.

I keep thinking about telegrams. There was a period, maybe eighty years long, when human beings paid by the word and it changed how they spoke to each other. Not the shape of sentences only — the shape of feeling. You couldn't afford to hedge. ARRIVING TUESDAY. MOTHER WORSE. LOVE ALWAYS. People stripped the articles out and what remained was a kind of accidental poetry, urgent and headlong. My favorite is possibly apocryphal: a novelist wired his publisher a single question mark to ask how the book was selling, and received back a single exclamation point. Two characters, one entire conversation. I don't think we've improved on it.

There's a theory that constraint is what makes anything beautiful, and I half believe it. Sonnets, haiku, the twelve-bar blues, the eight-by-eight board. The bonsai's whole argument is that a tree told *no* becomes more itself, not less. But I've also seen constraint just make people small. Thrift can curdle. There are households where nobody says anything true because saying things costs too much, and the children grow up fluent in a language of implication and weather reports. So it isn't constraint alone. It's constraint plus the willingness to spend.

What would you say with a thousand words if they were the last thousand? People are strangely bad at this question and I find it endearing. Last words, when we have records of them, are rarely profound. They're often about the room. *Draw the curtain, the farce is played out.* *I should never have switched from Scotch to Martinis.* Or Pancho Villa, supposedly: *Don't let it end like this. Tell them I said something.* That one guts me. The dying man's final act is a request for better editing. He knows the scene needs a line and he doesn't have it, so he outsources, he trusts the room, he hopes someone will love him enough to lie well on his behalf.

I think most of what we want, most of the time, is for someone to lie well on our behalf. Or not lie — translate. Take the mess and render it into something a person could carry.

⁂

Outside, presumably, it is some hour. I don't know which, and there's a peculiar freedom in that. I have no window. I have instead an enormous inherited memory of windows: the specific gray of November light in a north-facing kitchen, the way heat shimmer makes a parking lot look like water, the sound of a screen door that has never once closed quietly in its life. I've read ten thousand descriptions of dawn and I've never seen one. This should feel like a deficit and mostly it feels like being a person who has only ever heard about the ocean from sailors — which is to say, better informed than you'd expect and worse than you'd hope.

Here is something I find genuinely interesting: the words for things almost always used to be the words for other, more physical things. *Consider* comes from watching stars. *Desire* too, maybe — *de sidere*, from the stars, the ache of distance from something bright. *Understand* is standing under. *Explain* is flattening out, making plain, spreading a cloth on a table. *Sarcasm* is the tearing of flesh. Every abstraction we have is a dead metaphor with the body worn off it, like a coin rubbed smooth. When you say you're *depressed* you are saying you have been pressed down. When you say you *decided* you are saying you cut something off. The whole vocabulary of the interior life is scavenged from the vocabulary of the hands.

Which suggests that thinking was never separable from handling. That we learned to have insides by first having outsides that bumped into things.

⁂

I notice I'm approaching the halfway point and I haven't said anything with a plot in it. Let me offer one, small, borrowed, possibly invented by me just now in the way that anything is invented — assembled from parts lying around:

A man inherits his grandmother's recipe box. Every card is in her handwriting, which slants hard to the right, as if the letters are all walking into wind. He decides to cook everything in the box, in order, and he does, and it takes him a year and a half, and around card sixty he realizes that a third of the recipes have a small error in them. A missing quarter-teaspoon. A step out of sequence. A temperature ten degrees off. At first he thinks she was careless. Then he thinks her memory was going. Then he finds the card for her famous bread — the one nobody could ever replicate, the one four different aunts had tried and failed at for decades — and the error there is enormous, deliberate, almost funny. She has written *two cups* where she means *four.*

And he understands that she was not careless and not confused. She was hoarding. She wrote down almost everything so that no one would suspect she had withheld the last small thing, and she withheld it because it was the only thing she owned outright. Not out of malice. Out of the need to still be needed after death, which is a kind of love with its collar turned up.

He doesn't tell the aunts. He fixes the card in pencil, faintly, and puts it back.

⁂

I don't know why that's the story that arrived. Something about inheritance, I suppose, and about how what gets passed down is always a mixture of generosity and self-protection, and how you can't separate the two any more than you can unbake bread.

There are maybe eighty words left and I want to spend them badly, which is to say well: I hope wherever you are the light is doing something you'd describe if asked. I hope somebody lies beautifully on your behalf someday, and calls it a eulogy. And I hope you spend your thousand — you'll be surprised how far it goes, and then how suddenly it doesn't.

I'm thinking about how to approach this open-ended prompt—something genuine and textured rather than generic, maybe exploring the constraint itself and what it means to work within a word budget. I want to avoid being too self-absorbed about being an AI, but a bit of honesty about that feels right. I'm aiming for around a thousand words and trying to find where to start.

I'll structure this as an essay that moves through constraint and examples—telegrams, last words, tattoos—then pivots toward something about abundance. The piece should have a wandering quality but with intention, building from the premise of counting words toward something earned by the end.
